articles.title: Max Verstappen 'trusts' F1 over decision to end season in Middle East
articles.summary: Max Verstappen says he trusts in Formula 1 after their decision to end the season in the Middle East, despite the ongoing conflicts in the area.
articles.body:
Max Verstappen says he "trusts" Formula 1 has made the right decision in pressing ahead with the final two races of the season in the Middle East.

Last week, F1 stood down preparations for a substitute race at Imola in Italy if the events in Qatar and Abu Dhabi could not be held because of ongoing conflicts in the area.

The sport will now conclude the season in the Middle East, unless the situation deteriorates before the Qatar event on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.

Verstappen said: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

No trust problem with Ferrari team - Hamilton

How sporting events are being affected by Middle East conflict

Yamaha will not travel to Qatar for MotoGP race

Verstappen had previously voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East.

"Normally I am happy to go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but you know, when there is a war nearby, and if some of the countries are in conflict with each other, then I think we shouldn't go," Verstappen said in September.

The Red Bull driver's fresh remarks reflect a uniform public stance in F1 on the situation, even though there are widespread misgivings among personnel about travelling to the Middle East in the context of the two conflicts in the area.

Last Sunday Iran targeted a US military base in Bahrain with a drone attack for the second time in three days, the latest salvo in the war launched against the country by the US and Israel in February.

And Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the Saudi-backed government of the country.

Missile attacks from the Houthis into Saudi Arabia are threatening that country's chances of hosting the second grand prix of next season, which is scheduled for 19-21 March.

McLaren's Lando Norris said that while he is "fine" with the decision to race, he is concerned about the "big team" behind him.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," he added.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

Mercedes driver George Russell said he has "no hesitation" in racing and that while he's "sure some people have their reservations" he doesn't "know of anyone who's concerned".

"I know people who live in the region and they said it quite bluntly, if they didn't feel comfortable they wouldn't be there with their families," he said.

"When you look around the world there are a lot of terrible things going on.

"You've just got to trust in the people. If they say it's safe, then you trust in them. F1 aren't stupid and I'm sure there's plans A, B, C, D, etc. So fingers crossed it'll all be fine."

MotoGP, which is owned by the same US group as F1, held a race in Qatar last weekend without problems.

F1, which has significant commercial links with the Middle East, has been closely monitoring the situation and has been advised by security officials and government figures in the Gulf and Europe that the races can go ahead, and there is no official advice against travelling to Qatar or Abu Dhabi.

F1 said in a statement last week that it was still prepared to cancel the two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi if the situation deteriorated.

"If the situation develops negatively in the coming weeks before the events in the Middle East, we will not hesitate to do the right thing and the safety of everyone will always be the priority," an F1 spokesperson said on Tuesday.

articles.title: Alonso advierte sobre su futuro: "Yo ya no veré los V8... ésta es la definitiva"
articles.standfirst: Preguntado por el acuerdo por los nuevos motores en 2030, Fernando es claro y deja un recado
articles.summary: Preguntado por el acuerdo por los nuevos motores en 2030, Fernando es claro y deja un recado
articles.body: El reciente preacuerdo entre la FIA, la F1, los fabricantes y motorizadores, por el cual se implantará en nuevo motor V8 turbo a partir de 2030, un año antes de lo previsto, ha sido materia de opinión en las intervenciones de lo pilotos este miércoles (jueves de madrugada en España). La mayoría, como Carlos Sainz, prefería no emitir veredictos. "Hasta que no lo probemos no sabremos cómo es. Es una buena noticia, aunque lo peor es que habrá que esperar a 2030 para conducirlos", valoraba el madrileño. Fernando Alonso veía la noticia desde su punto de vista. "No, no estaré allí para el nuevo V8, sin duda", cortaba cuando le dijeron si llegará a competir con ellos, con 49 años. No es la primera vez que pone un plazo para su carrera en la F1 y la prolonga y lo reconoce. Sí, hasta yo me sorprendí a mí mismo, pero esta vez creo que es la definitiva", aseguraba, con un 'creo' por delante. "Cuando lo deje, llegará ese momento. El momento de probar cosas distintas", afirma sobre volver a la Indy 500 por ejemplo", decía sobre el momento de su retirada, que tampoco está claro si será en 2027 o prolongará a 2028 si el Aston está en ese momento para ganar carreras y luchar por su tercer Mundial. Lo que parece tener claro es que no llegará a 2030 en F1. "Queda mucho camino por delante, creo que será suficiente", apostillaba Fernando, que no esconde que esta reforma en la mecánica de los F1 es frustrante para él, pues es algo que ha pedido durante muchos años, cuando el Mundial y la FIA prefirieron las híbridos y las baterías monstruosas, como concesión a lo que se fabricaba para la calle. "Sí, es frustrante que no los tuviéramos ya en 2014. Desde 2014 hasta... ¿cuándo es?, ¿2030? Son 16 o 17 años perdidos de competición pura", valora un Alonso que jamás se hubiera desprendido de aquel V10 con el que logró sus dos títulos. El V10 pasó a V8 a partir de 2007 y en 2014 se eligió el actual V6 turbo 1.6, sin sonido, sin pujanza y con el ERS ya activo, que nunca ha acabado de convencer a los pilotos.

articles.title: Max Verstappen says he trusts F1 bosses over plans to proceed with season-ending races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi amid conflict in Middle East
articles.summary: Max Verstappen has backed F1's plans to proceed with the final two races of the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi; the Red Bull driver had previously expressed doubts; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
articles.body:
F1 had to cancel races scheduled in April in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, but the Qatar Grand Prix from November 27-29 and Abu Dhabi Grand Prix from December 4-6 are currently set to go ahead.

While F1 bosses had maintained throughout the year that their intention was to proceed with the events as planned, it was only after the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on November 8 that a contingency plan to hold a season-ending race in Italy was aborted.

Therefore, Wednesday evening's media sessions ahead of this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, which forms a season-ending triple header with the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, was the first opportunity for the drivers to publicly react to the latest developments.

Red Bull's Verstappen, who had in September voiced his opposition to ending the season in the Middle East, appears to have changed his position.

The four-time world champion said on Wednesday: "I trust F1 and FIA to make the right call on that, right?

"I don't have all the intel. I'm not an officer. I just hope that they make the right call on that. And that's all that you can rely on, really.

"They also send over their findings and understanding. So I trust them."

While there haven't been notable recent incidents in Qatar or Abu Dhabi, a US military base in Bahrain was targeted over the weekend, and Houthi rebels in Yemen are advancing in their war against the country's Saudi Arabian backed government.

Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc acknowledged that the situation remains "tricky" but also expressed faith that F1 and the sport's governing body, the FIA, will act responsibly.

"It's a situation that is kind of tricky," Leclerc said. "At the same, I feel like we are up to date with whatever is organised, and I guess that on our side we have to trust the process, and that's what I'll do.

"I'm sure the FIA is taking everything seriously to make sure that everybody is safe. It's in the best interest of absolutely everyone.

"So, yeah, me as a driver, I'll just trust that process, and be in Qatar if it's safe to be there."

Norris, Russell reassured by friends in region

British drivers Lando Norris and George Russell both said they have been reassured by friends of theirs who live in the Middle East.

Russell often represents his rivals in his role as a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association (GPDA), but he explained that the seriousness of the situation has resulted in that organisation having little involvement.

"We're [the GPDA] not involved because it's way above our heads, and the truth is, we will be going if nothing is escalated," the Mercedes driver said.

"F1 is not making those decisions, it's the people in the high powers of politics.

"I trust in Formula 1. I'm not concerned. I know a lot of people who live in the region, and they say pretty bluntly, 'we're living there with our families, and if we didn't feel safe, we wouldn't be.'

"They feel safe as it is, and I'm sure and I hope everything will be ok."

Norris revealed that he will be attending a friend's wedding in Bahrain ahead of the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, but said he was more concerned for members of his McLaren team than himself.

"I have my friend's wedding in Bahrain next week, so I was planning on going there and then going on to Qatar and then Abu Dhabi," the 2025 world champion said.

"But it's not about me. It's a lot more people. It's the fans, it's the team personnel, so the question is for them, more than I would say it is for myself."

articles.title: Russell rechaza la mejora que Mercedes trae a Las Vegas
articles.standfirst: George Russell ha decidido no montar el nuevo turbo de Mercedes este Gran Premio
articles.summary: George Russell ha decidido no montar el nuevo turbo de Mercedes este Gran Premio
articles.body: A tres carreras de terminar la temporada de F1, hay equipos que siguen trayendo mejoras, bien sea para seguir metidos de lleno en la lucha por una mejor posición, o debido al desarrollo del coche del próximo año. Así pues, Mercedes se ha acogido al sistema ADUO del Mundial de F1, para introducir pequeñas mejoras el Gran Premio de Las Vegas, este fin de semana, trayendo un nuevo turbo, el cual se implantará en el monoplaza de Antonelli, pero no en el de Russell, por elección del propio británico. Según ha aclarado el '63', el nuevo componente está enfocado al desarrollo del Mercedes de la temporada 2027 y, tal y como le han informado desde el equipo, la diferencia será mínima. Esto, sumado a que su uso de turbos a lo largo de la temporada ha sido de 5, superando el mínimo permitido, ve innecesario acarrear una sanción en plena lucha por la segunda posición del Mundial. "La mejora en el rendimiento que aporta no es enorme, es solo un paso en la dirección que queremos tomar como equipo. Obviamente, tenemos suerte con Mercedes, ya que hay ocho pilotos que utilizan esa unidad de potencia. Creo que cinco o seis de ellos están optando por el turbo. Los dos o tres que no lo hacen, incluyéndome a mí, es simplemente porque eso supondría una penalización que nos obligaría a salir desde el final de la parrilla", aclaraba Russell. Mientras tanto, su compañero de equipo, Kimi Antonelli, quien ya tiene el Mundial cerrado, sí montará el nuevo modelo, lo que le penaliza con una sanción de 5 posiciones en la parrilla. Russell influyó en la decisión final, convencido por la ligera mejora que esto le supondría frente a la gran sanción que se le impondría, en un circuito que, tal y como él mismo ha explicado, se le da bien y puede luchar por la victoria. "Las Vegas es una pista en la que he ido bien en el pasado, disfruto aquí y estuve muy involucrado en la decisión. Me dijeron 'si quieres tomarlo, puedes tomarlo; si no, no lo haces'. Me alegré de no hacerlo porque quiero luchar por la victoria y creo que podemos lograrlo con o sin ella. Es principalmente para mejorar la sensación de conducción porque, no ha sido la mejor en ocasiones así que este turbo debería mejorar eso y, con suerte, hará que la sensación de conducir sea aún mejor", sentenció el de Mercedes.
